about: Plain words for the small things a visitor can tap in a real (PDB) structure that are not one of the 20 amino acids or the DNA letters: metal ions, water, ATP and ADP, dyes, modified amino acids, sugars, drugs. Keyed by the wwPDB Chemical Component Dictionary code (label_comp_id). Every code found by tools/mol_het_scan.py across the 40 molecules has an entry (python tools/mol_het_scan.py --check). kind picks the tag and the shared sentences; recipe holds sentences for one structure only, read from that file's own crystal-growing record. lines is the key to the dashed lines Mol* draws in the close-up after a tap; colours read from Mol* 5.12.0 (vendor/molstar/molstar.js). Every sentence names its sources (s). No em or en dashes.

text.t: Proteins hold metal ions with oxygen, nitrogen or sulfur atoms of their amino acids, and the metals help with jobs such as holding the protein's shape, passing signals and speeding up chemical reactions.
Some small molecules in a structure are byproducts of the experiment rather than part of what was studied.

Calcium ion (Ca2+): a calcium atom that has lost two electrons, so it carries two positive charges.
Magnesium ion (Mg2+): a magnesium atom that has lost two electrons, so it carries two positive charges.
Zinc ion (Zn2+): a zinc atom that has lost two electrons, so it carries two positive charges.
Proteins usually hold zinc with four atoms around it, often from the amino acids histidine and cysteine.
Manganese ion (Mn2+): a manganese atom that has lost two electrons, so it carries two positive charges.
Iron ion (Fe3+): an iron atom that has lost three electrons, so it carries three positive charges.
In animals, iron held inside heme is what carries and stores oxygen.
Sodium ion (Na+): a sodium atom that has lost one electron, so it carries one positive charge.
Proteins usually hold sodium with six oxygen atoms around it.
Potassium ion (K+): a potassium atom that has lost one electron, so it carries one positive charge.
Potassium channels pick out potassium by wrapping it in eight oxygen atoms from the protein's backbone.
Mercury ion (Hg2+): a mercury atom that has lost two electrons, so it carries two positive charges.
Chloride ion (Cl-): a chlorine atom that has gained one electron, so it carries one negative charge.
Hydroxide ion (OH-): one oxygen and one hydrogen with an extra electron, so it carries one negative charge.
Phosphate ion: one phosphorus atom with four oxygen atoms around it, carrying three negative charges.
A water molecule: one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms.
Water molecules stuck to a protein are often important to how it works and what it binds.
ADP (adenosine diphosphate) is what is left when ATP, the cell's main energy currency, gives up one of its three phosphate groups to release energy.
ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the cell's main energy currency: breaking off one of its three phosphate groups releases energy the cell uses for its work.
Heme: a flat ring molecule with one iron atom held at its centre.
In animals, the iron in heme is what carries and stores oxygen.
Retinal: the light-catching part of rhodopsin in the eye.
When it absorbs light, one bond flips from a bent to an extended shape, which starts the signal to the brain.
Tetramethylrhodamine maleimide: a dye molecule.
The paper behind this structure says the actin was modified so it could not join filaments, and the file lists this dye among its keywords.
4-Methylhistidine: the amino acid histidine with one extra methyl group (one carbon and its hydrogens).
It is linked into the chain like any other amino acid, at position 73.
The chromophore: the light-emitting heart of GFP.
It forms by itself from three amino acids of the chain, threonine, tyrosine and glycine, which fuse into one new ring structure.
Selenomethionine: the amino acid methionine with its sulfur atom swapped for selenium.
Lysine with an extra carboxylic acid group on the tip of its side chain.
Phosphoserine: the amino acid serine with a phosphate group attached.
N-acetylglucosamine: a sugar unit built on a glucose ring.
Mannose: a sugar unit with six carbon atoms.
Mannose (beta form): a sugar unit with six carbon atoms.
Galactose: a sugar unit with six carbon atoms.
Fucose: a sugar unit with six carbon atoms.
Fucose (beta form): a sugar unit with six carbon atoms.
Nonyl glucoside: a glucose ring with a chain of nine carbon atoms attached.
2-Carboxyarabinitol 1,5-bisphosphate: a sugar-like molecule carrying two phosphate groups.
Acetic acid: a small molecule with two carbon atoms.
Ritonavir: a drug that blocks HIV protease, used to treat HIV infection.
Tacrine: a drug that blocks cholinesterase; it was used for Alzheimer's disease and has since been discontinued in the United States.

CA.t: Calcium acetate was in the liquid used to grow this crystal.

ZN.t: Zinc acetate was in the liquid used to grow this crystal.

HG.t: Mercury acetate was in the liquid used to grow this crystal.

ATP.t: ATP was added to the liquid used to grow this crystal.

intro.t: The sticks are the amino acids and other parts within 5 angstroms of what you tapped; solid sticks are covalent bonds, where atoms share electrons.
Dashed lines are weak attractions between atoms, not covalent bonds.

items.name: Blue: hydrogen bond
items.t: A slightly positive hydrogen atom pulled toward a slightly negative atom nearby.

items.name: Purple: metal coordination
items.t: A metal ion held by nearby atoms of the protein or of water.

items.name: Green, orange, teal: other attractions
items.t: Pi stacking (between rings), cation-pi (a positive charge near a ring) and halogen bonds, the other kinds Mol* looks for here.
